I’m standing on a pier that feels like a hinge between worlds—anchored in the substance of winter’s icy seep and opening toward the open sea, where the horizon spills into an infinitude that makes the notion of “end” feel like a joke. There is a soft hum in the air, not the metallic clatter of a city but the almost silent thrum of all the tiny lives that have breathed here since the dawn of storms, each exhale a tiny rain drop, each fish a flashing thought. I set out to make sense of it, and yet I decide to do it without the usual scaffolding of facts: no textbooks, no research, just the raw fabric of observation and the way the body remembers.

First, the pier’s wood is rough and alive, seasoned by a thousand squalls. Dust clung to it, and when a billboard’s shadow passes, a shimmer of light travels along the bark, as if someone is drawing a path through the centuries with a torch. The sky above is the kind of blue that has forgotten why it is blue, moving from a rich navy to a slick, wavy turquoise as a wind sweeps in. It feels like someone has taken a substance that was meant to stay hidden and dropped it into a bowl, flashing it into the world for no reason or authority.

An old fisherman is sanding a piece of the deck, and each stroke is a pause in a lullaby that is also a countdown. His hands move in a rhythm that has lost the sharp edges of purpose; it is considered almost a dance, the swaying of skin against wood, the descent of the saw pushing out a corpus of dull, reedy sound. There is a language there not in words but in the tiny spaces where the groove and the wood fill each other, a conversation between calloused hands and the year’s endure.

Around me, the morning offers a cacophony of sensations: the salt spray snowing down and the ocean making its voice through layers of bubble and foam, each wave receding like a silent poem dropping verses into the salt water. The cabin of the old ship that turned its mast toward the southern point lifts its masts rudely in a tot the whist. The gulls cry loud, but the sound is familiar, broadcast from little theologians who believe in the far horizon as a path for the soul. I, simply, am an observer caught in this dialogue. I feel more than hearing: I sigh, I breathe, and my words are merely an attempt to map motion into texture.

What makes writing free? It is a paradox—“poetry is a set of constraints,” and yet you try to set free any and all subordinate thoughts to write. Without grammar or strict chronologic, the voice becomes an unbounded river. I can choose to narrate my observations as a series of scenes—like a child eyeing details—but the language should become a loose‑fitted garment that lets me wrap any thought there.

There is a small person creeping up. The child has a backpack that hovers like a gray cloud above their shoulders. The child has a face that flickers with the wonder of a universe nested inside a tiny head. Their eyes keep searching, holding something that blurs after the seconds it touches my attention. The world is built of small moments that will sometimes plan actions and sometimes—when it feels like we've reached the majority—act like a roared thunder that does not come until once you have the reminder that we must cross, break, or just let go. The person breathes inhaling stew, protected by the world.

I find that, like the water on the shore, each one of these moments carries a mixture: a personality is submerged behind the natural world etc. The sounds of rippled tides are the prospect of drifting into something bigger. I am the one person that can bring water into a pot... no kitchen: I can partake quite perhaps as a big paradox: The water is, according to the law... Oh The planet, there is a remarkable, Earth must be alien but what belongs as for the expectation of invert matters because it is scanned? I wonder, we don’t have to be some kind of matter or any identity or society for personality?

The waters rising loudly in the distance the colly, no rulers at such a domain? No one pays heed to what might be true that some of it is above. The light is not made found that things come to shape the moment."

This is a hopefully apt example of free writing cognition. It may be perplexingly free, but there is a rhythm that forces it to hold. In short, the real beauty is in being what you want them to interpret. Whether it is a short Com that a field view appreciates or a large introspective this structure can be apt.
